newsitem.title: UK: Long-term survival in AIDS still poor, study finds.
newsitem.headline: Long-term survival in AIDS still poor, study finds.

text.p: AIDS patients may be living longer than before but their chances after five years are still slim, British researchers reported on Friday.
However new drugs and combination treatments introduced in the past two years offered much more hope and could transform such depressing figures.

Andrew Phillips of London's Royal Free Hospital and colleagues there and at Chelsea and Westminster Hospital looked at the cases of 2,600 AIDS patients treated at the two hospitals between 1982 and 1995 -- one of the biggest such studies ever.
"Median overall survival was 20 months; only one in 15 patients was alive five years after diagnosis (with AIDS)," they wrote in a report in the British Medical Journal.
But they found patients were much less likely to die in the first three months after being diagnosed with AIDS.
"In the first three months after diagnosis, patients in whom AIDS was diagnosed after 1987 had a much lower risk of death than patients diagnosed before 1987," they added.
Fifteen percent of all patients used to die within three months. That figure was five percent after 1987.
Phillips said it could be that drugs were keeping HIV-infected patients from progressing to AIDS as quickly as they used to.

"Since 1987 the AIDS survival has not changed very much, which does not sound particularly positive, but patients are being diagnosed with AIDS at a later stage of HIV infection," Phillips, an epidemiologist, said in a telephone interview.
"It appears that they are being kept healthy longer."
Phillips said doctors had changed their criteria for AIDS diagnosis and now did not consider a patient had progressed to "full-blown" AIDS until their immune systems were significantly damaged.

Phillips said he would expect the statistics to change even more as patients were treated with protease inhibitors and other new drugs that, in combination with older drugs like AZT, have been found to knock the virus back heavily.
"Protease inhibitors have become available and we expect that if we were able to analyse patients up to now we would hope that these survival rates would increase," he said.
"That's the kind of thing that we are going to move on and have a look at. I think there is a lot more optimism since 1995 which is not seen in this paper."
